# CLI Reference

The `idea` binary is both the CLI and the daemon. Output is styled with [Charm.sh](https://charm.sh)
(Lip Gloss, Huh, Glamour, Bubble Tea) when stdout is a terminal, and falls back to plain text when it
is piped, redirected or scripted.

## Commands

The table below is generated from the CLI's own command table — the same one `idea help` and the
dispatcher read. Run `make docs` after adding or renaming a command; `make docs-check` (and CI) fails
if this file has drifted.

## Flags and JSON output

Both columns above are generated from each command's flag specification in
`internal/cli/cli.go`, not written by hand. A flag that exists in the code cannot be missing from
this table: `make docs-check` fails if the two disagree.

The **Flags** column lists every flag a command accepts. Flags belonging to a subcommand are shown
with it (`add --type`), because each subcommand carries its own specification — `idea model ls`
does not accept `idea model add`'s flags.

The **`--json`** column is the contract:

- **`yes`** — the command prints the daemon's response for that endpoint as JSON on stdout and
  nothing else.
- **`no`** — the command takes flags, but none of them is `--json`. Its output is human-readable:
  a rendered artifact, or a confirmation line.
- **`takes no flags`** — the command itself accepts no flags. Its subcommands still may; the Flags
  column shows those.
- **`rejected`** — `plan` renders a markdown artifact, so there is no JSON form of it. It fails with
  a message pointing at `idea tasks --json` rather than ignoring the flag.
- **`—`** — a documentation row describing a subcommand, listed under its parent.

**`idea status` exits non-zero when it prints a failed initiative.** The reason travels with it,
on both paths — rendered for a human, and as `failure_reason` in `--json` — so a script can run it
as a health check and say why. An initiative merely waiting on your judgment is **not** a failure
and still exits 0: that is the loop working, and `idea next` names what it is waiting for.

**`--json` is the wire response, not the rendered view.** The two are not the same shape, and the
human form is usually the richer one: `idea status --json` emits the initiative list —
`[{"id","title","status"}]`, plus `"failure_reason"` on a failed initiative — while the rendered
form additionally composes requirement, decision
and question counts and the next-move guidance, each from a different endpoint. So a script cannot
assume every number it can see is in the JSON. The shapes themselves are
[`docs/openapi.yaml`](openapi.yaml)'s response schemas, by the endpoint each command calls
([`api.md`](api.md) maps command to route).

**Which initiative a bare command acts on.** Every initiative-scoped command takes an optional
initiative reference as its first positional argument, and an id that matches no initiative is an
error rather than a silent miss. With none, it acts on the **most recently created** initiative in
the project — not the one you last touched, and not one you selected. With several in flight, pass
the reference explicitly:

```bash
idea prd                         # the newest initiative
idea prd 4c1629f3382af9cd        # a specific one
```

`idea status` and `idea changed` take the same reference, and both are the overview when you omit
it: `idea status` lists every initiative in the project, and `idea changed` reports on the newest.

**Unknown flags are an error on every command.** So are unknown subcommands of `model`,
`executors`, `config` and `daemon`. Ten commands used to ignore what they did not recognise — 
`idea status --jsonn` printed human output to stdout and exited 0, which broke any downstream `jq`,
and `idea logs -n 200` silently showed the default 50 lines. Every command now parses its arguments
against the specification this table is generated from, and a test iterates that table so a new
command cannot be added without joining it.

## Watching progress in real time

The daemon logs **every model request** (stage, role, model, duration) and every review cycle to
`~/.local/share/idea-harness/daemon.log`. To watch it live:

```bash
idea logs -f        # tail the log
# or run the daemon in the foreground in its own terminal:
idea daemon         # then run `idea new` in another terminal
```

The web UI shows a **Live activity** feed (the same events, polled on a timer — see [`ui.md`](ui.md)).

## Apply and revert protect edits made outside the harness

`idea apply` refuses to overwrite a file you edited in the workspace after the agent ran (it
compares the workspace against the change set's pre-image). `idea revert` is the mirror at the
other end: it refuses to erase a file you edited *after* apply, by comparing the workspace against
the change set's post-image (review A3). Both write nothing when they refuse and both name the
files:

```
$ idea revert CHG-3
idea: revert refused: the workspace changed since CHG-3 was applied: src/app.js: it was edited in
the workspace after apply; discard (or stash) your edits to src/app.js, then revert again
```

The advice is **discard (or stash)**, never "commit" (review M4): committing does not change a
file's bytes, so it cannot make the byte-for-byte comparison above pass. If a *later* change set is
what actually touched the file (not a manual edit), the advice names it instead —
`revert CHG-4 first` — since discarding what is really CHG-4's own change would be wrong.

There is no `--force`. The change set stays `applied`; act on the advice yourself, then run
`idea revert` again. This is a synchronous `409`, not an operation that starts and fails in the
background — see [`api.md`](api.md#errors) for the exact contract. The refusal also records a
`stale_post` finding on the change set, at an observation (non-blocking) severity: it does not
block completing the initiative (`idea verify`), since it names a workspace-vs-post-image mismatch
to look at, not something a disposition resolves.

## How it works

The CLI is a thin HTTP client to the daemon (§29, D1). On the first state command it auto-starts a
detached daemon if none is running, then retries. The daemon is the single writer; the CLI never
mutates state directly.

Environment variables:

```text
IDEA_HARNESS_STATE   override the global state directory (default ~/.local/share/idea-harness)
IDEA_HARNESS_ADDR    override the daemon address (default 127.0.0.1:8787)
```

## Configuring providers

```bash
# List providers and their status (ready / missing key / not configured).
idea model

# Set the default model (provider/model).
idea model set gemini/gemini-3.6-flash

# Add a custom OpenAI-compatible provider.
idea model add groq --type openai --base-url https://api.groq.com/openai/v1 --key-env GROQ_API_KEY
```

Provider configuration is also available in the web UI under **Settings**.

## Example

```bash
mkdir my-product && cd my-product
idea init
idea model set ollama/llama3.1      # point at a local model
idea new                            # interactive Huh form
idea watch                          # follow the run live
idea prd                            # read the reviewed PRD in your terminal
```

The workflow runs asynchronously (Operations); `idea new` prints the new `initiative_id` immediately, and
`idea watch` follows it to completion.
